# Review and benchmark

How warnings get voted on, how reviewers earn a seat, and what the measurements do and don't show. Back to the [README](../README.md) or the [docs index](README.md). The rules are specified in [ARCHITECTURE.md](ARCHITECTURE.md#5a-review-stage).

**What the review does today:** it triages. Reviewers must agree on one thing: does this warning need a person? `settled` and `noise` both clear it, so a split between them is not disagreement. In real runs, reviewers still sent nearly every warning to the person. Items where they split are worth reading first. It reviews every warning, 40 to a call, so a real run of about 160 warnings takes 5 calls per reviewer. Reviewers vote at the same time, and a failed batch abstains only on its own warnings, which then come to you. On a real run of 162 warnings, two full reviews cleared 14 and 15, but only 5 of those were the same warning. A cleared warning is a weak signal, because batch neighbours and repeat runs both change the result.

**Batch size was tested.** The four review seats answered known cases at 6 per call, at 48 per call, and hidden among 34 real warnings at 40 per call. The panel dismissed no real issue in any condition (0 of 48, 0 of 48, 0 of 20) and every seat found at least 92% in the large batches, so 40 stays. Non-issues sent to the person rose from 5 of 24 to 14 of 40 on the same two topics, so large batches err toward caution. The hidden test used 12 cases, 4 of them real issues, repeated five times, so it is thin evidence. It does not show that warnings cleared on real runs were safe to clear.

**Grouped decisions.** When three or more warnings need you, the first review seat groups them into decisions and rates each one high, medium or low. Warning text stays word for word, and every warning stays in exactly one group, with any the model leaves out kept under "Not grouped". If grouping fails, you get the flat list. On a real run, Mistral turned 39 warnings into 11 decisions and Gemini, working alone, turned them into 8. Severity is one model's judgment, and both rated most groups high, so treat it as a rough order.

**Review seats follow the benchmark.** Seats go to calibrated providers, best score first. With at least three of them, only they vote, so fewer voters can mean a dismissal needs every voter. With fewer than three, the remaining seats fill by score, and with no benchmark, slot order stands. A failed provider never gets a seat. Seated providers can share one service, as Ollama Cloud carries all four today. If that service fails, votes are lost and warnings go to you, so nothing is cleared.

**Votes are not proof.** The review follows the JEV laws from `fraymus-arena`: bounded choices, independent members, no retrying for a preferred answer, and every result advisory. Agreement shows stability, not correctness. Votes never change the ledger.

**Benchmark.** Open **Benchmark** to score your providers on 48 warnings with known answers, sent through the real review prompt: 8 scenarios, 8 calls per provider. The main score is how often a provider is right about whether a warning needs a person. Clearing everything would score 67% and miss every real issue, so a provider counts as calibrated only if the bottom of its 95% range beats 67% and it finds at least 90% of the real issues. The panel's key number is real issues wrongly dismissed. One author wrote the set, and it covers short written scenarios, so scores describe this set and do not prove any single vote. Any change to the cases or the review instructions clears all calibration. On 2 November 2026, three real runs on the 6 providers that answered every case scored 92% to 100%. With calibrated seats, the panel dismissed 0 of 16 real issues and sent 4 of 32 non-issues to the person. Codex answered 5 of 8 scenarios in that run, then hit its rate limit. One real issue, a missing copyright takedown process, was dismissed by every provider but Mistral in that run, so one vote kept it from a shared blind spot. The answers live in `app/known_answers.json`, and reports stay on your machine in `benchmarks/`.

**A seat can outlive its score.** Seats come from the newest benchmark report. In a later control run at 6 per call, MiniMax found 41 of 48 real issues (85%), below the 90% needed for a seat, after scoring 94% in the report that seated it. The panel still dismissed nothing, because other reviewers caught those issues. Run the benchmark again after any provider or model change.

**First full chain with these seats.** On 2 November 2026, a real run was killed during stage 5 and resumed from the app. It finished all 16 stages on the first attempt, with all 20 review calls answered, 185 warnings arranged into 15 decisions, and a brief written. The review cleared only 3 of the 185, so expect nearly every warning to reach you.
